# EasyMesh Terrain Generation

EasyMesh builds the visual terrain around the road generated by `trackgen`.
It does not define simulation or collision geometry, which comes from the
loaded track XML. The visible road AC3D mesh is generated separately by
`GenerateTrack()`. The generic triangulation implementation is in
`easymesh.cpp`, TORCS domain construction is in `terrain.cpp`, and AC3D grouping
and export are in `terrainoutput.cpp`. Small testable checks remain in
`easymesh_checks.h`.

## Domains

Without an accepted grade-separated crossing, terrain is generated as two
triangulation domains:

- The interior domain fills the infield enclosed by the track.
- The exterior domain fills the area between the track and the configured
  terrain border.

Track orientation determines whether the outermost left or right track side
forms each boundary. `GenerateTerrain()` calls `generateTerrainDomain()` once
for each domain, then writes both into the same terrain output collection.

For a track with accepted crossings, `terraindomain.cpp` builds a planar
arrangement from the synchronized road ribbon and bridge, socket, and floor
footprints. `generateCrossingTerrain()` triangulates every connected free
domain discovered inside the terrain border, so the domain count is not fixed.

Relief lines add constrained chains to either domain. They guide
triangulation and elevation but are not themselves visible geometry.

### Crossing portal closures

All crossing parts belong to the track (`*-trk.ac`) output. At each corner,
`appendSocketPortal()` closes the
boundary between the rendered upper endpoint, underside/socket-top corner,
socket base, and rendered floor endpoint. Each adjoining strip ends in a single
edge regardless of its interior sampling density, so the usual closure has two
triangles per corner (eight per bridge). Near an aligned upper endpoint the
diagonal changes to preserve the underside vertex; collapsed faces are omitted.
Winding continues from the socket wall's existing end edge, including vertical
and near-vertical portals where a projected-area sign is unreliable.

The model separates the underside, right/left bridge fascia, right/left socket
walls, four portal fillers, and right/left floor strips. Export nests these
eleven polygon objects under bridge/socket groups within `TRKCROSS*`.
The usual vertical portal-extension triangle belongs to its upper-track fascia;
the remaining inclined triangle belongs to a separate `TRKFILLER*` object under
the corresponding lower-track socket group. The two letters in a filler name
identify the upper-track side first, then the lower-track side.

If the complete return lies in the fascia's vertical plane (within the renderer
point tolerance), it belongs to the fascia too. At an aligned upper endpoint,
the alternate diagonal splits the return into two faces; these stay together,
either in the fascia if coplanar or in the filler otherwise. A filler may thus
be vertical in this limiting case. These decisions use the construction's
endpoint/plane relationships, not a post-processing triangle-normal classifier.
Splitting parts retains triangle coordinates, winding, texture names and UVs.

The non-rendered `terrainMask` supplies the portal's exclusion footprint, not
its visible closure. The usual closure projects onto that same footprint; its
vertical triangle has zero projected area. Do not substitute the mask triangle
alone for the visible corner: it would omit the underside/socket-top vertex.
The floor's zero-gap check examines the actual crossing span, since rounding
can collapse an unrelated sampling-window endpoint's offset normal.

`test/trackgen/validate_crossing_seams.py` checks every crossing part's perimeter
against exported track and terrain edges in 3D, accepting subdivided edges.
It complements the projected-overlap checks in `validate_ac.py`.

### Crossing materials and texture coordinates

Crossing UVs are assigned after geometry construction. Mapping changes only
texture names and UVs, not vertex positions, winding, or terrain footprints.
These optional attributes in `Graphic/Terrain Generation` select entries in
the track's `Surfaces` section:

| Attribute | Default surface | Nominal U x V size |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `crossing bridge underside surface` | `bridge-underside` | 14 x 7 m |
| `crossing bridge side surface` | `bridge-side` | 14 x 7 m |
| `crossing bridge socket surface` | `bridge-socket` | 14 x 7 m |
| `crossing bridge floor surface` | `bridge-floor` | 4 x 4 m |

The default surfaces in `data/data/tracks/surfaces.xml` reference the matching
PNG files. A custom entry can specify independent physical repeat sizes:

```xml
<section name="my-bridge-concrete">
    <attstr name="texture name" val="my-concrete.png"/>
    <attnum name="texture size" unit="m" val="14"/>
    <attnum name="texture size v" unit="m" val="7"/>
</section>
```

Select it with, for example,
`<attstr name="crossing bridge socket surface" val="my-bridge-concrete"/>`
inside `Graphic/Terrain Generation`. `texture size v` is used by the crossing
mapper and defaults to `texture size`; existing road/terrain mapping is unchanged.
Missing/empty texture definitions fall back to the existing concrete material,
or to the adjacent lower-track boundary material for floors. An invalid U size
uses that fallback material's positive size; a missing/invalid V size uses U.
Version-3 tracks use their existing `Surfaces/List` lookup convention.

- **Underside:** U is the upper-track transverse axis (right to left), V is
  along the upper-track tangent at the crossing. The mapping is planar, starts
  at the projected footprint bounds, and crops a nominal tile on narrow decks.
  If the projected width exceeds the U size, both sizes grow by
  `max(1, width / sizeU)`. U stays within [0, 1]; V can repeat along the span.
- **Fascia and its vertical extensions:** U follows horizontal arclength along
  the sampled upper boundary. V follows global elevation and is anchored at 1
  at the highest point of the two fascia objects together.
- **Socket walls and fillers:** U follows the sampled socket boundary on walls.
  A filler uses its own horizontal face direction, with the U phase anchored
  to its socket corner, avoiding a collapsed projection at oblique returns.
  Both walls and all four fillers share one elevation reference and scale.
- **Vertical fitting:** each of the two families above includes its complete
  closure geometry in the height bounds. Both nominal sizes grow by
  `max(1, height / sizeV)`, preserving aspect ratio and keeping V within [0, 1].
  Smaller heights crop the image rather than squeezing a whole tile into each
  face. U is centered at the corresponding crossing station and may repeat.
- **Floors:** both strips share a lower-track-aligned planar frame, centered
  at the crossing. U follows the lower tangent and V points to its left.
  Both axes repeat at their configured sizes; strip width is not normalized.

The Windows data-setup script and both full NSIS installers explicitly include
all four PNGs. The Linux texture Makefile collects PNG assets automatically.
The regression fixtures have matching material definitions in their isolated
`test/trackgen/data/tracks/surfaces.xml` catalog.

## State and Ownership

`GenerateTerrain()` allocates one `TerrainGenerationContext` on the heap. It
owns the TORCS configuration and constrained input, one reusable `EasyMesh`,
and one `TerrainOutput`. Mesh topology and input are reset for each domain;
output groups persist until all domains have been written.

`relief.cpp` receives a bounded `tMeshInput` view when it appends relief points
and segments. It does not access EasyMesh globals or own those arrays. The
relief scene graph itself remains owned by the relief loader.

## Pipeline

Each legacy or crossing terrain domain performs these stages:

1. Build the domain rings and append relief constraints clipped to that domain.
2. `EasyMesh::generateMesh()` starts the generic triangulation pipeline.
3. `loadConstrainedMesh()` creates a containing triangle, inserts all
   constrained points, and records boundary chains.
4. `eraseOutsideDomain()` removes triangles outside the requested active domain.
5. The refinement loop processes active triangles until they are accepted,
   blocked, or the refinement budget is reached.
6. `countNodeNeighbours()`, `relaxConnectivity()`, and `smoothNodePositions()`
   improve connectivity and vertex placement without changing the constrained
   boundary.
7. `renumberMesh()` gives active nodes, elements, and sides compact output
   numbers.
8. `assignMaterials()` propagates terrain materials through unconstrained sides.
9. `TerrainOutput::append()` divides triangles into spatial AC3D objects and
   prepares their texture coordinates.

After all domains complete, `TerrainOutput::write()` writes the terrain objects
to the standalone mesh file and, when requested, the combined track file.

Object placement is a downstream operation. `GenerateObjects()` loads the
terrain mesh only when the track defines object maps; tracks without object
maps skip that potentially expensive model load entirely.

## Mesh Model

The triangulation context uses three indexed arrays:

- `Nodes` contains `tMeshNode` entries with coordinates, target `spacing`,
  boundary state, and output numbering.
- `Elements` contains `tMeshElement` triangles with three neighbours, three
  sides, quality values, and refinement state.
- `Sides` contains `tMeshSide` edges with adjacent elements, opposite nodes,
  length, and a constraint marker.

For each element, `nodeI`, `neighbourI`, and `sideI` correspond: the neighbour
and side are opposite that node. The same rule applies to the J and K fields.
For each side, `startNode` and `endNode` are the edge endpoints;
`oppositeNodeA` belongs to `elementA`, and `oppositeNodeB` belongs to
`elementB`.

`MISSING_MESH_INDEX` (`-1`) is both the missing-index sentinel and the marker
for an eliminated item. Code that follows neighbour indices must preserve this
distinction and use the checked access helpers where an index may be missing.

`RELIEF_BOUNDARY_MARK` is the opaque positive `INT_MAX` marker shared by relief
constraints and the rectangular terrain border. It is compared for identity
and is never used in arithmetic.

## Refinement

`classifyElements()` computes the active element to refine next. The local
target size is the average node `spacing`. `circumradius`, `inradius`, boundary
state, and neighbouring accepted triangles determine whether an element is
done or is the next candidate.

For a selected element, `tryInsertRefinementNode()` chooses a preferred side
next to an accepted triangle or constrained boundary. It then tries all three
element sides in deterministic order: preferred side first, followed by the
remaining sides in element order.

Each side attempt has one of three results:

- `REFINEMENT_INSERTED`: one finite node was inserted and the triangulation
  was updated.
- `REFINEMENT_BLOCKED`: that candidate was unusable without changing the
  mesh. Other sides are still attempted.
- `REFINEMENT_STOPPED`: an invariant or finite-geometry check failed. Further
  refinement stops, but finalization writes the current mesh.

If every side is blocked, the element is marked `refinementBlocked`. The mark
prevents repeatedly selecting an element that cannot make progress. It is
cleared only when node insertion or an edge swap changes that element's
geometry.

Candidate rejection is normal near constrained edges and complex boundaries.
It is not a reason to abort terrain generation. A coarser valid triangle is
preferable to no terrain mesh.

## Limits

The limits have separate purposes:

- `EASYMESH_MAX_NODES` is the physical capacity of the fixed-size triangulation arrays
  inside the heap-allocated context. The related element and side arrays have
  capacity for the topology created by that many nodes.
- `MAX_REFINEMENT_NODES` is the practical node budget for one domain. It
  includes constrained nodes already inserted by `loadConstrainedMesh()` as
  well as nodes added during refinement.

The refinement budget is lower because classification and finalization contain
large repeated scans. Allowing pathological domains to approach the storage
limit can take excessive time. Reaching the refinement budget stops insertion
and continues the normal finalization pipeline, producing a coarser mesh.
Interior and exterior domains each receive their own budget.

The storage limit remains necessary for initial boundary and relief geometry,
and as the final protection against array overflow. It is not a quality target.

## Output Safety

Spatial groups reuse vertices with identical coordinates. Before a surface is
stored, `TerrainOutput::insertElement()` rejects triangles whose local vertex
indices collapse and triangles that duplicate an existing surface in either
winding. This prevents repeated-vertex and duplicate AC3D surfaces even if
refinement leaves duplicate topology. The export guard does not replace full
geometric validation.

The regression validator in `test/trackgen/validate_ac.py` checks generated
terrain for finite coordinates, valid references, distinct triangle vertices,
duplicate surfaces, and non-zero area.

## Diagnostics

Detailed blocked-element and quality diagnostics are intended for developers
and are suppressed by `trackgen -q`. A stopped refinement reports that the
current mesh is being written. Users are not expected to repair individual
candidate failures.

`test/trackgen/run_regression.py` runs each fixture in a separate process with
a timeout. The EasyMesh helper tests are in
`test/libs/easymesh_test/easymesh_test.cpp`.

## Maintenance Invariants

Changes to refinement should preserve these rules:

- A blocked attempt must not mutate node, element, or side counts.
- A successful attempt inserts exactly one node.
- All three sides are tried before an element is persistently blocked.
- A topology change clears the affected element's blocked state.
- A recoverable failure or refinement limit still reaches AC3D export.
- Export never writes repeated-vertex or duplicate terrain surfaces.

Malformed constraints, allocation failure, or input larger than the fixed
storage capacity can still prevent generation. Those are input or resource
failures, not refinement-quality failures. Dynamic boundary and relief arrays
track their capacities explicitly; exceeding an allocation fails instead of
writing beyond the buffer.
